digest.intro: Blood in ancient bone, gold moving through shadow networks, and machines learning who you love.

items.title: Iran's nuclear proposal, Ukraine's pivot, and what the midterms just unlocked
items.blurb: Trump said he'll decide on resuming Iran strikes now that the midterms are over — and Iran has simultaneously sent a nuclear proposal via Qatar, contingent on the US meeting seven demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile Zelenskyy is openly recalibrating toward bipartisan US support rather than waiting on European consensus, which Peskov pointedly noted Europe can't yet articulate anyway.

items.title: West Africa's refinery wave: capacity built for gold that isn't theirs
items.blurb: Guinea, Burkina Faso, and Mali are building gold refineries with a combined claimed capacity of over 1,000 tonnes — against collective national output of fewer than 250 tonnes. The math only works if they're pulling in artisanal and smuggled gold from neighboring states, redirecting flows that currently exit through Dubai; Russia's Yadran Group holds a 38% stake in Mali's refinery, and Guinea has already banned raw gold exports and shipped its first refined bars in October.

items.title: Bambu H3C: nine tools, six seconds, the multi-material ceiling just moved
items.blurb: The H3C keeps nine independently pre-heated print tools permanently loaded and swaps between them in under six seconds — not a purge-and-reload, an actual tool change — in a footprint no bigger than a single-spool printer. It prints 75A TPU reliably, which has historically been the material that breaks every multi-material workflow. For anyone making physical things with more than one material, this is the most consequential desktop hardware announcement in years.

items.title: Apple quietly ships a family classifier in every Mac
items.blurb: Since macOS 13, every Mac has shipped two background daemons whose sole job is building a queryable knowledge graph of who you are, who you know, how you're related, where you go, and with whom — cross-referencing Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, and Screen Time. This graph is what Apple Intelligence's LLMs retrieve from, and it includes a relationship classifier that infers family structure from behavioral signals. It's on-device, but it was never disclosed, and you can now query your own.

items.title: 115-million-year-old dinosaur blood, confirmed by heme
items.blurb: Paleontologists found round blobs in the vascular channels of a juvenile Brazilian theropod's leg bone — and confirmed they're blood cells by detecting intact heme, the iron-bearing molecule in hemoglobin, inside the fossil but nowhere in the surrounding sediment. Heme surviving 115 million years extends the fossil soft-tissue record and opens a direct molecular window into dinosaur physiology that previously only existed in Crichton novels.

items.title: Person of Interest, 2026
items.blurb: Someone rewatched Person of Interest and wrote a quiet, bilingual essay about how a show that felt like science fiction in 2011 now feels like documentation — SOPA, Megaupload, the Machine, all of it landing differently when the surveillance infrastructure it imagined is simply ambient reality. The HN thread drew 154 comments not because it's technical but because it touched something; it's the kind of piece that makes you want to go rewatch the first season.

facts.fact: Burkina Faso opened a gold refinery with 164 tonnes of annual capacity — nearly double the country's entire national gold output of 94 tonnes.
Heme — the iron-bearing molecule inside hemoglobin — has been detected intact inside a 115-million-year-old dinosaur fossil, while the surrounding sediment contained none.

Apple's on-device personal knowledge graph daemons cross-reference Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, and Screen Time to infer family relationships — and have shipped on every Mac since macOS 13 without public disclosure.

art_picks.title: Mélodie en sous-sol (Any Number Can Win)
art_picks.creator: Henri Verneuil, 1963
art_picks.why: A heist film where the real subject is ritual and system: two men execute an elaborate scheme against a casino — a machine built to grind them down — with the whole thing held together by pure compulsive craft. The ending is one of cinema's great feedback-loop images. Pure signal for someone who loves invisible systems made suddenly, catastrophically visible.

art_picks.title: Myron Stout: Works on Paper
art_picks.creator: Myron Stout
art_picks.why: Stout spent years on a single painting, iterating obsessively on the tension between a form and its ground until it locked. His drawings are studies in how identity emerges from constraint — the kind of unreasonably narrow commitment that tends to hook you hard. No digital equivalent; purely physical.

art_picks.title: Selected Works
art_picks.creator: Visible Cloaks
art_picks.why: Generative electronic music that feels structurally akin to WebGL — shimmering feedback systems that never quite repeat, built from Japanese ambient tradition and a designer's attention to texture. The music sounds like a living render, which is either a great hook or a dealbreaker, and you'll know in 90 seconds.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt — Last Chance
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Huyghe worked with Kyoto neuroscientists to have an fMRI scanner record a person imagining images; a neural network then generated thousands of visual interpretations of those brain scans, displayed on freestanding screens in MoMA's outdoor garden — sensors detect visitors looking at the work, pulling it into a live feedback loop between human perception, biological data, and machine cognition. Last three weeks.

events.name: Art Week NYC — Inaugural Edition
events.venue: Citywide (Chelsea, Tribeca, LES, Upper East Side + 80+ galleries)
events.why: The first-ever citywide art week launched by Artforum, ARTnews, and Art in America — not a fair, but a coordinated crawl across 80+ galleries and 32 institutions including the Met, Guggenheim, Whitney, and Studio Museum in Harlem, all running openings and programming simultaneously; built to surface the gallery scene rather than a convention-center spectacle.

events.name: ADAA Fair 2026
events.venue: Park Avenue Armory, 643 Park Ave, Manhattan
events.why: The rebranded successor to the long-running Art Show, this iteration puts 63 peer-selected galleries into the drill hall with an emphasis on solo presentations and curated depth over booth-fair chaos — the architecture of the Armory alone earns it, and this edition is the first under the new ADAA Fair banner, so the energy is genuinely different.

events.name: Site Conditions: Five Talks on Art and the City (Art Week NYC × New Museum × Artforum)
events.why: Five back-to-back public conversations on Nov 14 covering AI and studio practice, the economics of making work in New York, artists moving into film, and how architecture shapes perception — with Ian Cheng, Aria Dean, Elizabeth Diller, Annabelle Selldorf, and Shohei Shigematsu among the speakers; dense and specific, the opposite of a panel.

events.name: The Superfair NYC
events.why: Emerging-artist-forward Brooklyn fair that bills itself as a corrective to the institutional art world — hundreds of cutting-edge works by emerging artists direct to a new generation of collectors; counterpoint energy to the ADAA week uptown, and worth checking if you want to see what's moving outside the established gallery system.

trial_sources.name: Chartbook by Adam Tooze
trial_sources.why: Columbia historian Adam Tooze writes several times a week at the precise intersection of geopolitics, economic history, and current events this reader craves — more freewheeling than his FT columns, more rigorous than anyone else operating at this frequency.

trial_sources.name: The Niche – Paul Knoepfler (ipscell.com)
trial_sources.why: UC Davis stem cell biologist Paul Knoepfler runs the web's most authoritative independent blog on regenerative medicine, covering stem cells, peptides, and longevity research with the credibility of an active researcher and the skepticism of a watchdog.

trial_sources.name: CNC Kitchen (Stefan Hermann)
trial_sources.why: Stefan Hermann brings genuine materials-science rigor to 3D printing — systematic tensile tests, filament comparisons, and print-parameter experiments that treat digital fabrication as engineering rather than hobbyism, making it the thinking-person's maker channel.
